Embeddings, in depth

Every embedding encodes a theory of what counts as the same thing. The theory came from somebody's training data, and once you have written crores of vectors to an index you have adopted it, whether or not anyone in the room could state it.

1. Two rooms, three weeks apart

On 11 August 2026, in a converted bungalow off Tonk Road in Jaipur that Kalasetu Bazaar still called its head office, Nandita Bhargava was looking at a chart she did not like. Kalasetu is a consumer marketplace for handloom textiles and craft goods: 2.4 lakh sellers, 61 lakh live listings, most of them written by artisans or by the small aggregators who onboard them. Nandita, who had joined from a large horizontal e-commerce company eighteen months earlier and worked out of Bengaluru three weeks in four, had shipped vector search across the whole catalogue in May. Search sessions were up. Gross merchandise value per search session was down 6.8 per cent.

The chart that mattered was a scatter of listings by rank position. Under the old keyword system, the listings that ranked first for "cotton saree for summer wedding under 3000" were the ones whose titles contained those words. Under the new system they were the listings whose titles read like every other listing — long, comma-separated strings such as "Cotton Saree Wedding Party Wear Designer Traditional Ethnic Summer Handloom Gift" — because sellers had spent five years learning to write for a keyword engine, and a text embedder trained on ordinary prose treats a listing crammed with the vocabulary of the whole category as a passable match for any query in that category. The engine was not broken. It was faithfully reproducing the distribution of the text it had been given.

Three weeks later, on 27 August, in an office tower in Lower Parel, Suhas Iyer faced a decision with the same shape and none of the same freedoms. Vidhaan Compliance Cloud sells obligation mapping to banks, non-banking financial companies and insurers: it ingests circulars and master directions issued by bodies such as the Reserve Bank of India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, decomposes them into individual obligations, and maps each obligation to the customer's internal controls. Twenty-two customers; 26 lakh indexed passages; a renewal worth ₹11.3 crore across the book in the following two quarters. Vidhaan's largest customer had asked, in an audit questionnaire, a question Suhas could not answer: when the system says an obligation is "not covered", what exactly has been searched, and how would we know if it missed something?

Suhas's engineering lead, Farida Qureshi, worked from Pune; the retrieval work was done by a two-person team in Kochi. Their options were the ones every enterprise team eventually lines up: continue with a commercial embedding API at ₹3.9 lakh a year in inference cost, fine-tune an open model on Vidhaan's own labelled obligation-to-control pairs at an estimated ₹42 lakh of engineering and compute, or abandon single-vector retrieval for something with a stronger audit story. Nandita and Suhas were solving the same problem in the same month. Almost nothing about the right answer was shared.

2. The idea, its history, and the camps that disagree about it

An embedding is a function from a piece of content to a fixed-length vector of real numbers, learned so that a chosen notion of relatedness corresponds to geometric proximity. Three parts of that sentence do the work. Fixed-length: the output size does not depend on the input size, which is what makes indexing and comparison tractable. Learned: the mapping is fitted to data, not designed. A chosen notion of relatedness: the training objective specifies which pairs should end up close, and everything downstream inherits that choice.

The intellectual line runs further back than most product teams realise. J. R. Firth's "you shall know a word by the company it keeps" (1957) is the distributional hypothesis on which everything rests. Gerard Salton's vector space model at Cornell in the 1970s made documents into vectors of weighted term counts, giving us cosine similarity and, later, the BM25 weighting that still refuses to die. Latent Semantic Analysis (Deerwester, Dumais and colleagues, 1990) applied singular value decomposition to the term-document matrix and produced the first genuinely dense, low-dimensional document representations — the direct ancestor of what we now call an embedding, and worth remembering because its failure modes are ours. Word-level neural embeddings arrived with Mikolov's word2vec in 2013 and Pennington's GloVe in 2014. Contextual representations followed with ELMo and BERT in 2018, which meant a word's vector could finally depend on its sentence. Sentence-level embeddings good enough for retrieval came with Reimers and Gurevych's Sentence-BERT in 2019, and the current generation — trained with contrastive objectives on hundreds of millions of mined text pairs — dates from roughly 2021 onward.

Around this history sit five camps whose disagreements are substantive rather than stylistic, and a competent product leader should be able to state what each will and will not sign.

The dense-single-vector camp holds that one good general embedder plus enough interaction data beats domain-specific engineering. It will sign: "for most corpora, a frontier general embedding model outperforms a small model fine-tuned on ten thousand in-house pairs." It will not sign: "one vector per document is sufficient for high-stakes retrieval."

The lexical-hybrid camp — the intellectual descendants of BM25 — holds that dense retrieval systematically fails on rare terms, identifiers and exact phrases, and that fusing a sparse keyword score with a dense score is close to free. It will sign: "on any corpus with proper nouns, codes or numerals, hybrid beats dense alone on recall." It will not sign: "keyword search is a legacy technology."

The multi-vector / late-interaction camp, whose reference point is ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020), holds that compressing a passage into one vector is an information bottleneck, and that keeping one vector per token and comparing at query time recovers what pooling destroys. It will sign: "single-vector pooling loses fine-grained term-level evidence that matters for long or heterogeneous passages." It will not sign: "the storage and latency cost is negligible" — it is typically ten to thirty times the index size.

The domain-adaptation camp holds that the general model's notion of similarity is simply the wrong notion for specialist corpora, and that a few thousand well-chosen in-domain pairs move the needle more than any amount of model shopping. It will sign: "fine-tuning on in-domain query-passage pairs with mined hard negatives reliably beats the base model on in-domain evaluation." It will not sign: "the fine-tuned model will generalise to queries unlike your training pairs."

The reranking-first camp holds that embeddings should be treated as a cheap recall device and nothing more, with all precision supplied by a cross-encoder that reads the query and candidate together. It will sign: "the marginal return on embedding quality above a decent baseline is smaller than the return on a reranker." It will not sign: "you can skip the recall stage" — a reranker cannot rescue a candidate set that never contained the answer.

These camps are not describing different systems. They are describing different beliefs about where the error lives — in the representation, in the vocabulary, in the pooling, in the domain, or in the ranking — and each is right on the corpora its proponents work with.

3. Mechanics in depth

Modern text embedders are trained contrastively. Given a batch of query-passage pairs, the model is asked to score each query highest against its own passage and lower against every other passage in the batch. The standard loss, InfoNCE, is the negative log of the softmax probability of the correct pair, with a temperature parameter that controls how sharply the model is punished for near-misses. Two design choices inside this recipe determine most of the model's behaviour, and neither is visible from the outside. First, what counted as a positive pair in the training data: title-and-body pairs from web pages teach a very different notion of "related" from question-and-answer pairs from forums. Second, how negatives were chosen: with only in-batch random negatives, the model learns to separate topics; with mined hard negatives — passages retrieved by an earlier model that look right but are not — it learns to separate answers from near-answers, which is the discrimination retrieval actually needs.

Pooling is the step teams skip in conversation and pay for in production. A transformer emits one vector per token; a passage embedding must be one vector. Mean pooling averages them, which is robust and topic-dominated. CLS pooling takes the vector at a designated summary position, which is sharper but only if the model was trained that way. Last-token pooling is standard for decoder-based embedders. The consequence of averaging is quantifiable: in a 200-word passage containing one decisive twelve-word sentence, that sentence contributes roughly six per cent of the mean. This is precisely why long chunks retrieve badly on specific questions, and why the fix for a specific-question failure is more often a chunking change than a model change.

The formal treatment is simpler than its reputation. If vectors are normalised to unit length — and virtually all text embedders are used this way — then cosine similarity, dot product and Euclidean distance are the same ranking function under different names, because for unit vectors ‖a − b‖² = 2 − 2·(a·b). A cosine of 0.85 is a Euclidean distance of √(2 − 1.70) = √0.30 = 0.5477. Anyone arguing about the choice of metric on normalised vectors is arguing about nothing; anyone using unnormalised vectors with cosine, and then wondering why long documents behave oddly, is arguing about something real.

Two second-order effects deserve names. The first is anisotropy: trained embedding spaces are not isotropic clouds but narrow cones, so random pairs of English sentences typically score 0.6 to 0.8 against each other rather than near zero. This is why absolute thresholds are meaningless and only margins carry information. The second is the feedback loop: whatever the retriever surfaces is what users click, and clicks become the training data for the next retriever. Kalasetu's keyword-stuffed listings ranked first, were clicked because they ranked first, and would have been labelled as positives by any naive click-mining pipeline — teaching the next model that keyword-stuffing is what buyers want.

Finally, storage. The index is not free, and the arithmetic is worth doing in public. Vidhaan's 26 lakh passages at 1,536 dimensions in 32-bit floats occupy 26,00,000 × 1,536 × 4 bytes ≈ 15.97 GB before index overhead. Truncating to the first 512 dimensions — possible without retraining if the model was trained with Matryoshka representation learning, which orders dimensions by importance — brings that to 5.32 GB. Quantising those 512 dimensions to 8-bit integers brings it to 1.33 GB, twelve times smaller than where we started. Kalasetu's 61 lakh listings at 1,536 float32 dimensions is 37.5 GB; binary quantisation at one bit per dimension is 1.17 GB, a thirty-two-fold reduction. Neither compression is free, and the cost is measured in recall.

This pattern — retrieve wide and cheap, then re-score narrow and expensive — is the single most reliable structural move in the whole field, and it recurs at every level from quantisation to cross-encoder reranking.

4. When the idea applies, and when it is actively misleading

The conditions under which embedding-based retrieval earns its complexity can be stated as testable claims. Claim one: the vocabulary gap is real. Users express the same need in words the corpus does not contain. Test it by taking two hundred logged queries and measuring what fraction have zero exact-term overlap with their correct answer. At Kalasetu the figure was 34 per cent — buyers write "for a summer wedding", sellers write "party wear". At Vidhaan it was 9 per cent, because compliance analysts search using the regulator's own vocabulary, having read the circular. The gap that justifies dense retrieval is three times larger at the consumer marketplace.

Claim two: the unit of retrieval is semantically coherent. Embeddings assume the chunk is about something. A Kalasetu listing is; a Vidhaan master direction spanning forty pages of numbered sub-clauses, cross-references and schedules is not, until it has been decomposed. Test it by asking a domain expert to read fifty random chunks and say what each is about; if they cannot, no embedder can.

Claim three: approximate recall is acceptable. Every production vector index misses things. Test it by asking what happens when the correct passage is not retrieved. At Kalasetu, a buyer sees a slightly worse saree and buys it anyway. At Vidhaan, an obligation is silently reported as not covered, and a bank's audit committee is told a falsehood by a system nobody can interrogate. This is exactly the question Vidhaan's customer asked, and it is not a question about embeddings at all — it is a question about whether a probabilistic recall device belongs in a control environment that expects completeness.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. When the query is an identifier — a UHID, a GSTIN, a circular reference number like DOR.CRE.REC.18/2026-27 — semantic similarity ranks things that are about the same subject above the one document that is the thing. When the distinction that matters is logical rather than topical — negation, quantity, date ranges, "excluding", "other than" — embeddings place the two sides of the distinction almost on top of each other. And when the corpus is small: below roughly ten thousand passages, a well-tuned keyword system plus a cross-encoder over all candidates is usually both better and cheaper, and the vector index is architecture theatre.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product companies the temptation is a single shared embedding space across products, owned by a platform team. It halves the cost and creates a coupling nobody planned: the platform team cannot upgrade the model without simultaneously re-indexing every product, and every product's relevance regressions land in the platform team's queue. The mature pattern is a shared service with per-product model pinning — each product declares which model version its index was built with, and migrations are per-product events with their own evaluation gates.

Two-sided marketplaces have the structural problem Kalasetu ran into: two populations write the corpus and the queries, with different incentives. Sellers write to be found; buyers write to describe need. Embedding both with a model trained on neither produces a space organised around whichever side wrote more text — always the sellers. The serious fix is to stop embedding seller prose as the primary signal and instead embed a normalised representation the marketplace controls: attributes extracted from the listing, the category taxonomy, and, where available, the buyer-side language that historically converted for that item. This is a supply-side policy decision dressed as a retrieval problem, and it fails when the search team owns retrieval but the catalogue team owns listing quality.

In regulated settings the binding constraint is not accuracy but explicability and residency. A bank's auditors will accept a recall figure if it is measured against a documented, version-controlled test set; they will not accept "the model thought these were similar." Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the sectoral guidance banks operate under, a vector derived from personal data is generally treated as personal data — which means an embedding index inherits deletion obligations. Deleting a person's records from a source database while their vectors remain in an HNSW graph, where deletion is typically a tombstone rather than a removal, is a real and commonly overlooked exposure. Vidhaan's answer was to partition indexes per customer and rebuild rather than tombstone.

Hardware and on-device products face a different squeeze. An embedding model small enough to run on a mid-range Android handset sold in India — say a 22-million-parameter, 384-dimension model — produces a materially weaker geometry than a server-side 1,536-dimension model, and the gap is largest exactly where Indian consumer text is hardest: transliterated Hindi, code-mixing, and regional-language input in Latin script. Teams that benchmark on English test sets and ship to a Tier-2 audience discover this after launch.

AI-native products invert the question. When retrieval feeds a generative model rather than a human, precision matters more than it appears to, because an irrelevant retrieved passage does not get scrolled past — it gets read, believed and woven into a fluent answer. The organisational seam here is brutal: the retrieval team measures recall@10 and reports success; the users experience confident wrong answers caused by the three irrelevant passages inside that ten.

6. Ten nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Similarity is a training-objective artefact, not a property of the content

The tell-tale sign in the wild is a team comparing two models by looking at their scores rather than their rankings on a labelled set. The obvious reading — that similarity is measured — is wrong. It is asserted, by a model whose assertion was fitted to whatever pairs its makers called positive. An expert's first question about an embedding model is not its benchmark score but what its training pairs were.

Anisotropy makes absolute thresholds a category error

The sign is a configuration file containing min_score: 0.75. Because embedding spaces occupy a narrow cone, the mean pairwise similarity between unrelated sentences can be 0.7 in one model and 0.2 in another. The obvious reading, that a higher score means more relevance in some transferable sense, is wrong. Experts calibrate thresholds per model against a labelled set, and treat any threshold as invalidated by a model change.

Recall and precision fail at different stages and need different owners

The sign is a single relevance metric on a dashboard. Recall is lost at chunking and at the approximate index; precision is lost at ranking. Teams that track one number cannot tell which they are losing, and typically spend their model budget on the stage that was not the problem.

Hard negatives, not model size, are the cheapest quality lever in fine-tuning

The sign is a fine-tuning project that reports disappointing gains and proposes a bigger base model. Training with random negatives teaches topic separation, which the base model already had. Mining negatives from the top-50 retrieved-but-wrong passages typically produces a larger jump than a model two sizes up, at a fraction of the cost.

The index is a snapshot in a coordinate system, and coordinate systems are not portable

The sign is a roadmap item reading "evaluate newer embedding model" with no re-indexing line item beneath it. Vectors from two models cannot be compared, mixed or migrated incrementally; the corpus must be re-embedded wholesale, and during the migration two indexes must be maintained. Experts cost this at the moment of first adoption, not at the moment of upgrade.

Asymmetry between queries and documents is a modelling choice, not a detail

The sign is a system whose long, well-formed queries work better than short ones, or the reverse. Symmetric models are trained so that two similar documents are close; asymmetric models so that a question and its answer are close. Many providers require a prefix — a literal string such as "query: " or "passage: " — and omitting it silently degrades results by several points of recall with no error anywhere.

Popularity and length biases enter through the corpus, not the model

The sign is that the same handful of passages appear in the top ten for unrelated queries. Passages written in the average register of the corpus sit near its centroid and are therefore near everything. This is what happened to Kalasetu's keyword-stuffed listings. The diagnostic is to compute how often each passage appears in the top ten across a thousand queries; a healthy corpus has a long flat tail, a sick one has a spike.

Evaluation sets rot, and rot invisibly

The sign is a test set built once, at launch, that every subsequent model passes. Query distributions shift with the product; a set built from launch-week queries stops representing the users within two quarters. Experts refresh a fraction of the set each quarter from live logs and keep the old set as a regression guard.

Multilinguality is not a checkbox but a geometry question

The sign is a multilingual model deployed for Indian-language search with no cross-lingual test. A model can be multilingual in the sense of handling many languages while placing the Hindi and English expressions of the same idea in different regions of the space. What matters is whether the space is aligned across languages, and the test is direct: embed five hundred translated pairs and measure how often each is the other's nearest neighbour.

Retrieval quality is bounded above by the chunking, and nobody budgets for chunking

The sign is a team on its third embedding model with flat metrics. If the answer to a question spans a chunk boundary, no retriever can return it. Experts run a cheap ceiling test: measure what fraction of labelled answers are fully contained within a single chunk. That fraction is the maximum recall the system can ever reach, and at Vidhaan it was 0.79 before the team changed how master directions were split.

7. How the practice differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the corpus is written by many hands, the queries are short, and behavioural data is abundant. The dominant lever is not the embedder but what you choose to embed and what you learn from clicks. In B2B and enterprise the corpus is specialised and small, behavioural data is scarce — Vidhaan sees perhaps four thousand searches a day against Kalasetu's eleven lakh — and the dominant levers are domain adaptation, chunking and hybrid retrieval. Platforms and marketplaces add the two-sided incentive problem described above, which no amount of model quality addresses. In hardware and on-device contexts the binding constraint is model size and the resulting geometry, and the honest answer is often to embed server-side and cache. For AI products where retrieval feeds generation, precision in the top five matters more than recall at fifty, which reverses the metric most retrieval teams optimise.

Where the difference is not real is worth saying plainly. The need for a labelled evaluation set is identical across every product type and stage; so is the requirement to cost re-indexing before adoption; so is the fact that thresholds do not transfer between models. These are not enterprise concerns or consumer concerns. They are consequences of what an embedding is.

Stage changes two things. Early-stage companies should use a hosted general model and spend their scarce attention on whether anyone wants the feature; the re-embedding cost at ten lakh documents is a weekend. Late-stage companies with crores of vectors, contractual uptime and an audit function should treat embedding choice as an architectural commitment with a documented exit path, and should run the evaluation-set work before, not after, committing.

The first example is the ordinary case of domain adaptation working. Vidhaan's compliance analysts had, as a by-product of five years of delivery work, 18,000 pairs linking an obligation sentence to the control text that satisfied it. Fine-tuning a 335-million-parameter open embedder on those pairs lifted nDCG@10 from 0.512 to 0.671 — a 31 per cent relative improvement that no commercial general model matched on this corpus. The second example is the cheap follow-on that most teams never run: re-mining negatives from the fine-tuned model's own top-50 mistakes and training again added another 0.053, for less than a third of the original cost. The generalisable lesson is that the second training run, not the first, is where the return is.

The third example is the one that failed. Kalasetu spent ₹64 lakh and four months replacing keyword search with dense retrieval over seller-written titles, and lost ₹15 per search session. The failure was not in the model, the index or the engineering; it was in the choice of what text to embed. Seller titles had been optimised against a keyword engine for five years, which meant they were not descriptions of products but bags of category vocabulary — and a bag of category vocabulary is, to an embedder, a decent match for every query in the category. The recovery took eleven weeks. Kalasetu stopped embedding titles as the primary signal and instead embedded a constructed string: the extracted attributes (fabric, weave, occasion, price band, region of origin), the category path, and the first two hundred characters of the seller's description with the title's duplicated terms removed. GMV per session went to ₹237, above the pre-project baseline. The organisational lesson mattered more than the technical one: the catalogue team, which owned attribute extraction, had not been part of the search project.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Centroid domination. The early warning is a small set of passages recurring in the top ten across unrelated queries. The diagnostic question: what is the distribution of top-ten appearances across the corpus? Caught early it is a chunking or content-normalisation fix costing weeks; caught after a marketplace's sellers have adapted to it, it is a supply-side re-education problem costing quarters.

Silent model drift on a hosted API. The early warning is relevance metrics moving without a deployment. Providers update models behind stable endpoint names more often than teams assume, and a changed model means new query vectors compared against old document vectors. The diagnostic: embed a fixed canary set of one hundred strings weekly and compare against stored vectors; any deviation beyond floating-point noise is a model change. Caught late, the entire index is quietly misaligned and nobody can date the onset.

Evaluation-set leakage into fine-tuning. The early warning is in-domain metrics that improve implausibly while user-facing metrics do not move. The diagnostic: check whether test queries or their near-duplicates appear in the training pairs. The cost of catching this after a customer commitment is credibility rather than money.

Deletion debt in the index. The early warning is a growing gap between source-of-truth record counts and index counts. The diagnostic: reconcile weekly. In a regulated corpus this is a compliance exposure that a customer audit, not a dashboard, will find.

Optimising recall while the user experiences precision. The early warning is a retrieval dashboard that is green while support tickets describe wrong answers. The diagnostic: sample twenty generated answers and count how many retrieved passages in each were actually used and actually relevant.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does domain fine-tuning still pay? The steelman for no: frontier general embedders are now trained on such breadth that a small team's 18,000 pairs mostly teach the model idiosyncrasies of its own labellers, and every fine-tune creates a model you must host, monitor and re-train as the corpus shifts. The steelman for yes: Vidhaan's numbers above are real, and no general model saw regulatory obligation language paired with bank control descriptions, because that pairing exists nowhere on the public internet. What would have to be true for the fine-tuning camp to be wrong: that the gains vanish on queries unlike the training pairs. Vidhaan has not tested this, and neither have most teams that report fine-tuning wins.

Is hybrid retrieval a permanent architecture or a transitional patch? The steelman for permanent: exact identifiers and rare terms are a structurally different retrieval problem, and no amount of dense-model progress makes a vector a good way to find DOR.CRE.REC.18/2026-27. The steelman for transitional: learned sparse models already fold lexical matching into a single trained system, and maintaining two retrieval paths with a fusion step is an operational tax. The evidence favours permanence today; the position would be wrong if learned-sparse systems became as cheap to operate as an inverted index.

Do single vectors have enough capacity? The multi-vector camp's evidence is consistent gains on long, heterogeneous passages. The single-vector camp's counter is that those gains largely disappear once a cross-encoder reranker is added, at a tenth of the storage cost. What would settle it is a comparison at fixed total system cost rather than fixed retrieval architecture — an experiment few teams run because it crosses budget lines.

Should embeddings be treated as personal data? The conservative position holds that a vector derived from a person's text is derived personal data and inherits every obligation, including erasure. The permissive position holds that a 1,536-number projection is not reasonably reversible and treating it as personal data makes vector search unworkable in regulated sectors. Published inversion attacks have recovered substantial portions of short source texts from embeddings, which has moved the weight of expert opinion toward the conservative reading; it is not settled, and Indian jurisprudence under the 2023 Act has not yet tested it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four observable ways. They ask what a model was trained to consider similar before they ask how it scores on a leaderboard. They refuse to discuss relevance without a labelled set in the room, and they treat building that set as product work rather than as a research chore delegated downward. They cost the exit — the re-indexing bill and the dual-index migration window — at the moment of adoption, so that "try a new model" is a decision with a known price rather than an argument. And they locate errors before proposing fixes: chunking ceiling first, then recall at the index, then ranking, then generation, because the cheapest fix is usually at the earliest stage and the most expensive model change is usually at the latest.

The person who has merely studied the topic can define an embedding correctly and will still buy the model with the best benchmark, tune a threshold that will not survive the next upgrade, and be surprised in the third month.

12. What each decided, and three questions

Nandita stopped treating the problem as a retrieval problem. Kalasetu kept the same embedding model and changed what it embedded, moving from seller titles to a constructed representation built from extracted attributes and the category path, with the seller's own description as a secondary signal. Her reasoning was that the model's notion of similarity was defensible — it was the corpus that had been corrupted by five years of incentives, and no model would fix an incentive. She also moved attribute-extraction coverage onto the search team's own scorecard, which was the harder change.

Suhas answered his customer's audit question rather than his engineering question. Vidhaan fine-tuned the open model, added a BM25 path for circular references, and — the part that actually satisfied the auditors — published a versioned evaluation set of 340 analyst-labelled queries with recall measured and dated for every release, alongside a written statement that the system's output is a ranked recall aid and not an assertion of completeness. The ₹11.3 crore renewal turned on the second document, not the first.

Three questions in the manner of a teaching note. First: Kalasetu's failure cost ₹64 lakh and was caused by embedding text that its own incentive system had degraded — at what point in the project should someone have asked what the corpus was optimised for, and whose job was it to ask? Second: Vidhaan's auditors accepted a documented recall figure of 0.991 and rejected an undocumented one of 1.000 — what does that tell you about what enterprise buyers are actually purchasing when they buy AI features? Third: both companies discovered that the decisive choice was what to embed rather than which model to embed it with. If that is generally true, what should a product organisation stop doing?

13. Going deeper

Tokens and tokenisation matters next because the tokeniser decides how your domain's rare words are fragmented, and fragmentation is the first place a general model loses your vocabulary. The transformer and attention explains why a token's vector depends on its neighbours, which is the mechanism that makes context-sensitive similarity possible at all. What a large language model actually is puts the embedding in its place: an internal representation exposed as an output, not a separate technology. Vector search and similarity is the immediate sequel — how HNSW and IVF find neighbours among crores of vectors, and what approximation costs, which is the recall column in Table 1. Chunking and retrieval quality is, on the evidence of both cases here, where more improvement lives than in model selection. Multimodality extends the same geometry to images and audio, and unlocks the marketplace question of searching a photograph of a weave. The context window governs how many retrieved passages can actually be used once you have them. Inference versus training clarifies why embedding a corpus is a capital expense and querying it is an operating one. Pre-training, post-training and fine-tuning gives the vocabulary for the domain-adaptation debate in section 10. RLHF and alignment matters less for embedders directly but explains why generation behaves differently from retrieval. LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning is the practical route by which a team fine-tunes an embedder for lakhs rather than crores. Quantisation is the arithmetic behind the last two rows of Table 1, and the reason a 37.5 GB index can become 1.17 GB.

Yogyata Talent Cloud: The Night Before the Board

Pune, Sunday 15 November 2026. A hiring-technology company has built a ₹96 crore business on a number that nobody can now explain, a vendor contract that expires in six weeks, and an index of 2.6 crore résumés that would cost ₹1.4 crore to rebuild.

1. Sunday night, Baner

Ishaan Deshpande had been Chief Product Officer of Yogyata Talent Cloud for four years, and he had never before printed a board pre-read and then failed to send it. The deck sat on the dining table of his flat in Baner, twenty-two pages, dated 15 November 2026, with a slide titled "Matching Quality: Path Forward" that he had rewritten six times since Thursday and that still said four different things depending on which exhibit the reader looked at first.

The board met at eleven the next morning at the Bengaluru office, with two directors dialling in from Singapore and one from London. Three decisions had converged on that meeting. The company's embedding vendor wanted a renewal signature by 31 December on a contract worth ₹2.1 crore a year. Al Reem Holding, a Gulf industrial group that was Yogyata's second-largest customer at ₹7.4 crore a year, had a renewal on 31 January and had sent a nine-page assurance questionnaire that Yogyata's legal head could not fully answer. And Meghna Rao, the chief executive, wanted the Series C conversation opened in February on the strength of a product story that Ishaan was no longer sure he believed.

At 9.40 p.m. a message arrived from Dr. Sujatha Iyengar in Toronto, where it was eleven in the morning. It read: "Before tomorrow — please look at the thing I sent about the templates. It isn't a model problem. I keep saying this and it keeps coming back as a model problem."

2. How the company got here, and the decision that boxed it in

Yogyata was founded in Pune in 2019 by Meghna Rao and Karthik Balasubramanian, both formerly of a large Indian IT services firm, on an observation about their own industry: a services company or a global capability centre receives lakhs of applications a year, and the bottleneck is not sourcing but reading. Their product ingested a customer's applicant database, its job descriptions and its historical hiring, and returned a ranked shortlist for any open role.

By November 2026 Yogyata served 148 enterprise customers, mostly Indian IT services firms, GCCs in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune, and staffing companies in India, the Gulf and the United States. Annual recurring revenue was ₹96 crore, growing 34 per cent year on year. Headcount was 214 across Pune, Bengaluru, Toronto, Berlin, Singapore and New Jersey, frozen since August pending the Series C.

The decision that constrained everything happened in the first quarter of 2023, and at the time it looked like unambiguous good judgement. Facing a build-or-buy choice on the matching engine, Karthik chose to represent every résumé and every job description as an embedding — a fixed-length list of 1,536 numbers produced by a hosted model, positioned so that documents the model considered similar sat close together — and to rank candidates by the cosine similarity between the job description's vector and each candidate's. It shipped in eleven weeks instead of the nine months a structured skill-extraction system would have taken. To secure volume pricing, Yogyata signed a three-year committed-spend agreement with the model vendor: ₹6.4 crore in total, expiring 31 March 2027.

Two further choices from that period turned out to matter more than the first. Yogyata exposed the cosine similarity to users as a Fit Score out of 100, rescaled by a fixed linear transform. Recruiters loved it; it entered their workflows, their internal reporting and, eventually, two customer contracts. Al Reem Holding's master services agreement and Ridgeline Staffing Partners' US contract both contain service credits payable if the mean Fit Score of delivered shortlists falls below 78 in a quarter, with a combined maximum exposure of ₹1.1 crore a year. Nobody at Yogyata in 2023 had understood that a Fit Score is not a property of a candidate but a coordinate reading in one particular model's space, and that changing the model changes every reading at once.

The second choice was a single shared vector index across all customers, built so that Yogyata could sell an anonymised "market talent insights" module. It worked commercially. It is also the subject of question 4.2 of Al Reem's assurance questionnaire.

3. The industry around it

Indian white-collar hiring in 2026 was a market of enormous volume and thin margins. Naukri, operated by Info Edge, remained the default job board; LinkedIn dominated the passive-candidate segment; Foundit and a dozen others competed below them. Yogyata did not compete with any of these — it sat on top of them, ranking what they delivered — but it competed with the in-house tools that TCS, Infosys and Wipro had built, and with the matching features that global applicant-tracking suites bundled at effectively zero incremental price. NASSCOM's own commentary through 2026 had been consistent: the industry's hiring problem had shifted from volume to relevance, and from relevance to retention.

Three regulatory forces bore on the product. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, gave candidates rights over their personal data, including erasure — and an embedding derived from a résumé is, on the conservative reading Yogyata's legal head had adopted, derived personal data that inherits those rights. Yogyata's shared index used a tombstone mechanism for deletions, which removes a vector from search results without removing it from the graph. Second, Nordwind Mobility GmbH, a Berlin-headquartered customer worth ₹3.1 crore, had written in September to ask how Yogyata proposed to meet the EU AI Act's obligations for AI systems used in employment decisions, which it classified as high-risk and subject to documentation, human-oversight and record-keeping requirements. Third, Al Reem operated partly out of the Dubai International Financial Centre, whose data-protection regime imposed its own cross-border and segregation expectations.

Roughly 38 per cent of Yogyata's revenue was earned outside India, from customers whose regulators asked harder questions than its Indian customers did, and whose renewals were larger.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Fit Score shipped in March 2024 and was, by every measure Yogyata tracked, a success. Median time from job posting to first shortlist fell from 6.2 days to 2.1. Recruiter satisfaction, measured by a thumbs-up control on each delivered shortlist, ran above 70 per cent from the second quarter onward and was still running there in October 2026 (Exhibit 2).

In August 2025 the team added "Similar Candidates": from any shortlisted profile, a recruiter could ask for the ten nearest neighbours in the vector space. It became the most-used feature in the product by clicks, and it is the feature Sujatha Iyengar's Sunday-night message referred to.

The first contrary evidence arrived on 19 February 2026, when the talent analytics team at a large Hyderabad GCC sent Priya Nambiar a slide of their own making. Candidates hired through Yogyata-generated shortlists had 90-day retention of 84 per cent against 93 per cent for employee referrals, and 12-month retention of 71 per cent against 88 per cent. Offer-acceptance rates were also lower. Priya escalated it; Greg Salvato in New Jersey pointed out, correctly, that referrals outperform every channel everywhere and that the comparison was unfair; the matter was noted and not pursued.

In June 2026 Sujatha ran a thirty-day A/B test of an open embedding model fine-tuned on Yogyata's own history of job-description-to-hired-candidate pairs. The results (Exhibit 5) are the most-cited and least-understood numbers in the company. On day 19, after the initial metric showed no movement, the primary metric was changed from recruiter thumbs-up rate to shortlist-to-interview conversion, and — because a configuration error had put some accounts in both arms — the control group was re-randomised on the same day. The test reported a 4.1 per cent relative improvement. Greg's deck says "no significant improvement." Sujatha's memo says "the test was not able to answer the question."

On 6 October, Farhan Sheikh in Pune found the thing that was hardest to explain to customers. Yogyata's weekly canary — a hundred fixed strings re-embedded and compared against stored vectors — had been failing silently since 14 July because the alert routed to a deprecated channel. The vendor had updated the model behind a stable endpoint name. For six weeks, incoming job descriptions had been embedded with a newer model and compared against candidate vectors produced by the older one. The two are different coordinate systems. Retrieval during that window was, in Karthik's phrase in the incident review, "confidently arbitrary."

Nobody can now say how much of the February-to-October drift in downstream outcomes was caused by the July-to-August window, because the customer data in Exhibit 3 was aggregated quarterly and the window sits across a quarter boundary.

Then, on 28 October, Sujatha's analysis of the Similar Candidates feature. Taking 4,000 pairs of candidates that the model placed within the top ten of each other, she and an analyst in Toronto hand-coded what the two profiles actually shared. In 61 per cent of pairs the strongest shared feature was résumé format: the same section headings, the same phrasing of responsibilities, the same two-column layout. Kaushalya Manpower Services, a staffing vendor supplying three of Yogyata's largest customers, formats every candidate it submits on one template. Those candidates were systematically each other's nearest neighbours, and systematically nearest to job descriptions written in a similar register. An embedding of a résumé, Sujatha wrote, is an embedding of a document — and a document's dominant regularity is how it was written, not who wrote it.

5. The people

Ishaan Deshpande, Chief Product Officer, Pune. Owns the recommendation going to the board. Believes privately that the product's core abstraction was wrong from 2023 and that saying so out loud in front of the investors, six weeks before a Series C process, would be an act of self-harm. He has not told Meghna that he has been approached by a competitor.

Meghna Rao, Chief Executive, Bengaluru. Position: renew the vendor, upgrade to their newest model, put "next-generation matching" in the Series C narrative, and fix the rest in 2027. Incentive: the round. What she is not saying is that the term sheet conversation she has had informally values the company on ARR growth and gross margin, and that a nine-month rebuild consumes both.

Dr. Sujatha Iyengar, Head of Data Science, Toronto. Position: the ranking should be driven by structured extraction — skills, years, verified employers, credential checks — with embeddings demoted to a recall stage that widens the candidate pool. Incentive: she has argued this since 2024 and has been overruled twice. What she is not saying is that her own June A/B test was compromised and that she knows it cannot bear the weight her memo places on it.

Karthik Balasubramanian, co-founder and VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: renew, re-index, recalibrate, and stop relitigating 2023. Incentive: he made the original architectural decision and has a frozen headcount of 214. What he is not saying is that the re-index of 2.6 crore profiles has never been done end-to-end and that his estimate of seventeen days is extrapolated from a 4 per cent sample.

Priya Nambiar, Customer Success Director, Singapore. Position: whatever keeps Al Reem. Incentive: 40 per cent of her variable compensation is APAC and Gulf net retention. What she is not saying is that Al Reem's head of HR technology told her in October that they had begun a parallel evaluation of an in-house build with a systems integrator.

Greg Salvato, SVP Sales, New Jersey. Position: do not touch the Fit Score. Incentive: US staffing renewals in Q1, and two contracts with service credits tied to the score. What he is not saying is that his largest US account has already asked why a candidate's score changed by nine points between two weeks in August.

Nikhil Saraf, Head of Legal and Compliance, Mumbai. Position: the shared index must be partitioned per customer before any renewal is signed, and the deletion mechanism must actually delete. Incentive: he is the person who signs the assurance responses. What he is not saying is that he does not know whether the DPDP position on derived vectors would survive a determined challenge, and that no Indian authority has yet tested it.

Jonas Weber, Principal Product Designer, Berlin. Position: remove the numeric Fit Score entirely and replace it with evidence — the three specific overlaps between candidate and role that drove the match. Incentive: he owns the Nordwind account's design relationship and has read the EU AI Act's oversight requirements more carefully than anyone else in the company. What he is not saying is that he does not know whether the system can produce that evidence, because a cosine similarity does not decompose into reasons.

  4. The June A/B test is cited as evidence by three people who disagree with each other. What, if anything, can legitimately be concluded from Exhibit 5? What would it cost Yogyata to have run a test that could be concluded from?
  5. Sujatha argues that the problem is what is being embedded rather than which model does the embedding. If she is right, which of the four paths in Exhibit 6 changes anything — and what fifth path does her argument imply?
  6. It is Monday morning. Ishaan has ninety minutes with the board and one recommendation. What should he do, in what order, and with what money? What should he say to the board about the six weeks in July and August, about Exhibit 3, and about what the company will know by 31 January that it does not know today?

Sunday, 11.40 p.m.

Ishaan opened Sujatha's attachment again. It was a single page: forty pairs of candidate profiles the system had called near-identical, with the shared phrases highlighted in yellow. On page one, two candidates from different cities, different employers, seven years apart in experience, sharing eleven consecutive words of a responsibilities bullet that Kaushalya Manpower put on every résumé it submitted.

He thought about Karthik's argument, which was not stupid: that the model was doing exactly what it had been built to do, that 148 customers were paying ₹96 crore a year for it, and that companies do not rebuild their core abstraction six weeks before a fundraise on the strength of forty highlighted résumés and a spreadsheet from two customers. He thought about Greg's 74 per cent, which was real. He thought about Meghna's message, which was also, in its way, correct.

Then he thought about the question from Dubai, which had been asked politely and was still unanswered: strong compared to what? He had four paths on a slide and no sentence to put under them. At 11.40 he closed the deck without sending it and went to look for a pen.
exp20v2-aivocab.embeddings:
Embeddings

A fixed-length list of numbers that stands in for a piece of content, arranged so that things the model considers alike sit close together. The phrase that matters in that sentence is the model considers.

1. Bannerghatta Road, 4 February 2026

Meera Raghavan had been Vice President of Product at Akshar Health Cloud for nineteen months when the Pune pilot went sideways. Akshar sells a clinical documentation platform to mid-sized hospital chains: doctors dictate or type their notes, the platform stores them, and administrators pull them back for insurance claims, audits and quality reviews. Forty-one hospitals used it. The company had 2.1 crore clinical notes in storage and was adding roughly nine lakh a month.

The new feature was called Ask the Chart. Instead of hunting through a patient's file, a doctor would type a plain-language question — has this patient had chest symptoms before? — and the system would surface the three or four notes that answered it. Akshar had signed a ₹6.4 crore, three-year agreement with a Pune hospital group contingent on the feature clearing a pilot. In the first four weeks of that pilot, 38 per cent of searches returned nothing the doctor found useful, and the hospital's chief medical information officer had started forwarding examples to Meera personally.

The examples were not random. A query about a patient's breathlessness returned a note about a ward's air-conditioning complaint. A query about post-operative infection returned the consent form for the operation. Devansh Kulkarni, who ran engineering, was clear that nothing was broken in the ordinary sense: the pipeline ran, latency was 240 milliseconds at the ninety-fifth percentile, no errors in the logs. Ritika Bose, the data scientist working from Hyderabad, put the problem more precisely on a call that Wednesday. "The system is retrieving exactly what we asked it to retrieve," she said. "We asked it for the notes that are most similar to the question. It is giving us those. We never agreed on what similar means, and neither did the model we borrowed it from."

The decision in front of Meera was narrow and expensive. Akshar could keep the general-purpose embedding model it was calling over an API at ₹0.42 per thousand notes; it could switch to an open medical-language model that Ritika would host on Akshar's own machines at roughly nine times the engineering cost and four times the latency; or it could spend six weeks building something it did not yet have — a set of a few hundred real doctor questions with the correct answering notes marked by a clinician — before choosing anything at all. Dr. Anand Shenoy, the retired physician who advised the product team two days a week, wanted the six weeks. The sales team wanted a fix by the end of the month.

2. The idea, stated precisely

An embedding is a fixed-length list of numbers — a vector — produced by a model from a piece of content, in such a way that content the model treats as similar produces lists of numbers that are close together in a geometric sense. The list is always the same length for a given model, whether the input is a four-word question or a two-page discharge summary: 384 numbers, or 768, or 1,536, or 3,072, depending on the model. Each number is called a dimension. Individually the dimensions mean nothing you could name. Collectively their pattern is the model's compressed opinion about what the content is about.

The problem embeddings were invented to solve is old and specific: computers match strings, and meaning is not a string. A search built on exact words cannot know that angina and chest tightness on exertion point at the same clinical thought, and it cannot know that chest X-ray machine service log does not, despite sharing the word chest. Gerard Salton and his group at Cornell proposed representing documents as vectors of word counts in the 1970s — the vector space model — which handled some of this by treating documents as points in space rather than bags of characters. The modern version arrived in 2013, when Tomáš Mikolov and colleagues at Google published word2vec, which learned a few hundred numbers per word from nothing but the company each word kept in a large corpus. The idea that a word's meaning could be recovered from the words that surround it was not new — the linguist J. R. Firth had put it as "you shall know a word by the company it keeps" in 1957 — but word2vec made it cheap. Sentence-level and document-level embeddings followed once transformer models arrived in 2017; by 2019 the sentence-transformers work of Nils Reimers and Iryna Gurevych had made high-quality paragraph embeddings routine, and by the early 2020s every major model provider sold them as an API call.

The sentence Meera could say in a room without sounding glib: "An embedding turns a piece of text into a point in space, and the model decides where that point goes. Our search is only as good as that model's idea of what belongs near what — which is a judgement about our domain, not a fact about mathematics."

3. How it actually works

Start with the note. Akshar's notes run from forty words to four thousand, so the first step is chunking: cutting each note into passages short enough for the model to handle and coherent enough to stand alone. Ritika's pipeline cut at 200 words with a 40-word overlap. That is a choice, and it is the reason a discharge summary's diagnosis line sometimes ended up in a different chunk from the symptoms that justified it.

Each chunk is then tokenised: broken into sub-word units the model recognises, drawn from a fixed vocabulary of perhaps fifty thousand pieces. Common words are single tokens. Uncommon ones are assembled from fragments — a general-purpose tokeniser is likely to split echocardiogram into three or four pieces, which is not fatal but tells you the word was rare in the model's training data. Every token is looked up in a table that assigns it a starting vector; this is the humble original sense of the word embedding, before it came to mean the whole-passage kind.

The transformer then does the work that makes the result worth having. Layer by layer, each token's vector is revised in the light of the other tokens present — the mechanism called attention. After this pass, the vector sitting over the word chest in "chest tightness on exertion" is not the same vector as the one over chest in "chest X-ray machine service log." Context has been folded in.

What comes out is a vector per token, not per passage, so the fourth step pools them into one — usually by averaging, sometimes by taking the vector of a designated summary token. This is a lossy compression, and it is where most of the model's opinion gets exercised: a 200-word passage with one clinically decisive sentence and 190 words of boilerplate will produce a vector dominated by the boilerplate, because averaging does not know which sentence mattered.

Finally the vector is normalised — rescaled so its length is exactly one — and written into an index. Normalising matters because it makes the comparison depend only on direction, not on magnitude, so that a long note and a short note about the same thing can score as close. Comparison itself is then the cosine similarity: multiply the two vectors element by element, add up the results, and divide by the product of their lengths. The answer runs from −1 to 1, and for normalised text embeddings it almost always lands between about 0.3 and 1.0, which is a fact with consequences we will come to.

4. The arithmetic, worked

Real vectors have hundreds of dimensions and no dimension has a name. To see the mechanics, take a deliberately fake four-dimensional version of Akshar's problem in which the dimensions happen to be interpretable. Call them, loosely, cardiac, symptom-report, paediatric and administrative. The doctor's query is Q = "patient reports tightness in chest when climbing stairs", which the domain-trained model places at [0.75, 0.60, 0.05, 0.15]. Three stored chunks compete: A, an old note reading "chest pain on exertion" at [0.80, 0.55, 0.10, 0.20]; B, a cardiologist's line reading "angina during walking" at [0.78, 0.50, 0.08, 0.25]; and D, the decoy, "chest X-ray equipment maintenance log" at [0.40, 0.10, 0.05, 0.75].

Take Q against A. Multiply term by term: 0.75 × 0.80 = 0.600; 0.60 × 0.55 = 0.330; 0.05 × 0.10 = 0.005; 0.15 × 0.20 = 0.030. The dot product is 0.965. The length of Q is the square root of (0.5625 + 0.36 + 0.0025 + 0.0225) = √0.9475 = 0.9734; the length of A is √0.9925 = 0.9962. Divide: 0.965 ÷ (0.9734 × 0.9962) = 0.995. The same arithmetic gives Q·B = 0.9265 and a cosine of 0.988, and Q·D = 0.475 with a cosine of 0.569.

Vectors are four-dimensional illustrations, not measurements. The margin row is the number that decides whether a retrieval system holds up under real queries.

Now change exactly one input: the model. Swap the domain-trained embedder for a general-purpose one whose training corpus was mostly web text, in which angina appears rarely and mostly in Latinate medical registers rather than alongside descriptions of walking. That model places B not at [0.78, 0.50, 0.08, 0.25] but at [0.55, 0.40, 0.10, 0.55] — closer to the formal-medical-document region than to the symptom-report region. Redo the arithmetic and B's cosine against Q falls from 0.988 to 0.864. Meanwhile D, whose language is ordinary English the general model knows well, rises from 0.569 to 0.649.

Notice what did and did not change. The ranking is identical: A, then B, then D. A demonstration on three examples would show no problem at all. What collapsed is the margin — the gap between the worst correct answer and the best wrong one — from 0.419 to 0.215. Margins are what absorb the noise of real queries: typos, hybrid Hindi-English phrasing, a doctor writing "SOB o/e" for shortness of breath on exertion. Halve the margin and a system that ranked perfectly on the demo starts placing decoys above answers on roughly the fraction of queries that happen to be a little unusual. Thirty-eight per cent, as it turned out.

5. Nuances a learner has to absorb

Similar is not a property of the text; it is a verdict by a model

This is the whole topic in one line. Two passages are close because a particular model, trained on a particular corpus up to a particular date, learned to place them close. Change the model and the distances change, as Table 1 shows without any change to the underlying notes. There is no neutral, model-free notion of similarity available to be measured. When someone says "these documents are 87 per cent similar," the honest completion of the sentence is "according to this model."

Absolute scores mean nothing; only ranks and margins do

Because of how text embedders are trained, almost all pairs of real English sentences score somewhere between 0.6 and 0.9 against each other. A cosine of 0.82 is not "82 per cent relevant"; it may be the best match in the corpus or it may be junk, depending entirely on what the alternatives scored. Any threshold — "show results above 0.75" — that was tuned on one model is meaningless on another, and teams that hard-code such thresholds discover this the week they upgrade.

An embedding compresses, and compression discards

A 200-word passage carrying perhaps 260 tokens is reduced to 768 numbers. Most of what survives is topic and register. What tends not to survive is negation, quantity and exact identity: "no history of diabetes" and "history of diabetes" embed very close together, because they are about the same subject in the same register. For a clinical product this is not a curiosity, it is a patient-safety issue, and it is the reason serious retrieval systems combine embeddings with exact keyword matching rather than replacing it.

The index is a photograph, and photographs age

Vectors are computed once and stored. If Akshar changes its embedding model, every one of the 2.1 crore stored vectors is now in a different coordinate system from newly computed queries, and the whole corpus must be re-embedded. Ritika's estimate for a full re-index was eleven days of compute and about ₹18 lakh. Teams that treat model choice as a switch they can flip later have not costed the flip.

Retrieval quality is decided at chunking as much as at embedding

The best model in the world cannot retrieve a fact that was split across two chunks so that neither chunk contains both the fact and the context that makes it findable. Akshar's 200-word cut separated some diagnoses from their symptoms. Debates about which embedding model to buy frequently turn out, on inspection, to be debates that chunking would have settled more cheaply.

Asymmetry between question and answer is real

A doctor's question and a clinical note are different kinds of text: different length, different register, different grammar. Some embedding models are trained specifically so that a question and its answer land near each other; others are trained so that two documents about the same thing land near each other. Using the second kind for question-answering means comparing a question to notes on the basis of whether the question reads like a note, which it does not.

What embeddings cannot tell you, however well you use them

An embedding cannot tell you whether a passage is true, recent, authoritative, or permitted to be shown to this user. It has no notion of the patient identity attached to a note, so nothing about embedding similarity prevents a chunk from another patient's file scoring highest. Access control, recency and authority are separate filters that must be applied around the vector search, and every serious deployment applies them before, not after, the similarity ranking.

The questions a thoughtful newcomer should ask

Three of them earn their keep. What text was this model trained on, and does it resemble ours? What would we measure to tell whether it is working — and do we have that measurement today, or only demos? And if this model turns out to be wrong for us, what does it cost in money and days to change it? A team that cannot answer the third question has bought an option it cannot exercise.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the corpus is usually large, the queries short and repetitive, and the tolerance for a mediocre result high — a shopper shown a slightly wrong pair of shoes scrolls on. The winning move is therefore usually a general model plus a large volume of behavioural feedback: what people clicked teaches the ranking more than any change of embedder would. In business-to-business software like Akshar's, the corpus is smaller, the vocabulary is specialised, the queries are long and the cost of a wrong answer is borne by a professional who will complain in writing. Here domain fit dominates, and the general-model-plus-clicks strategy fails because there are not enough clicks: forty-one hospitals generate a few thousand searches a day, not a few million.

Marketplaces sit awkwardly between the two, because they have two corpora that must be embedded into the same space — what buyers type and how sellers describe things — and sellers write to game search while buyers write to describe need. A marketplace that embeds both with one general model discovers that the space is organised around seller vocabulary, since sellers wrote most of the text. The fix is not a better model but separate treatment of the two sides, which is an organisational decision before it is a technical one.

Stage changes the calculus in one specific way. An early-stage company should almost always start with a hosted general model, because the dominant risk is that nobody wants the feature, and re-embedding ten lakh documents later is a real but survivable cost. A large company with crores of documents, a compliance function and a re-indexing bill measured in weeks should treat the choice of embedding model as an architectural commitment on the order of choosing a database, and should therefore insist on the evaluation set before committing rather than after.

7. Common mistakes

Demo-driven selection. The symptom from outside is a product that performs beautifully in the sales meeting and poorly in the pilot. The underlying misunderstanding is that a handful of queries chosen by the person who built the system tests ranking, when what matters is margin across the awkward tail of real queries. The cheapest diagnostic costs an afternoon: take fifty queries from the actual logs, not from imagination, and have a domain expert mark the correct answer for each. Any model that gets the top result right on fewer than about two-thirds of those is not going to be rescued by tuning.

Thresholds copied across models. The symptom is that a system upgraded to a "better" embedding model suddenly returns nothing at all, or returns everything. The misunderstanding is that a cosine score is comparable across models. The diagnostic is to plot the distribution of scores for a few hundred queries under both models; if the histograms sit in different places, every threshold in the code is now wrong.

Treating negation as a detail. The symptom is confident, fluent, wrong answers on questions of the form "has this patient ever…" The misunderstanding is that embedding similarity captures logical content. The diagnostic is to construct twenty deliberately paired passages differing only by a negation and check how often the wrong member of each pair outranks the right one. In most general models it is close to half.

Skipping the exact-match path entirely. The symptom is that a search for a specific identifier — a UHID, a drug batch number, an invoice reference — returns things that are merely about the same topic. The misunderstanding is that semantic search supersedes keyword search rather than complementing it. The diagnostic is to search for a string you know exists exactly once and see whether it comes first.

8. What good looks like

A team handling Meera's decision well does something unglamorous first. Before comparing models, it builds an evaluation set: two hundred to five hundred genuine questions, drawn from logs and from watching users, each paired with the passages a qualified person judges to be correct answers. This costs weeks and produces no feature. Everything afterwards becomes cheap and decidable: two models can be compared in an afternoon; a chunking change can be shown to help or not; an upgrade can be defended to a hospital's clinical governance committee with a number rather than an anecdote. The team also keeps a keyword path alongside the vector path and merges the two result lists, so that exact identifiers and negations have somewhere to go. And it writes down the re-indexing cost at the moment it chooses a model, so that the choice is made with its exit price visible.

9. What Meera decided

She took Dr. Shenoy's six weeks, and shortened them to four by narrowing the scope. Rather than a general evaluation set, the team assembled 220 questions from the Pune pilot's own logs — the ones that had failed — and had Shenoy and two resident doctors mark the correct notes. Against that set, the general model returned a correct passage in the top three for 61 per cent of questions; the medical model, for 84 per cent. Two changes that cost nothing did nearly as much work as the model swap: cutting chunks at section boundaries in the note template rather than at 200 words lifted the general model to 72 per cent, and adding a keyword path for identifiers and negated phrases lifted the combined system to 89 per cent.

Meera's reasoning was that the ₹6.4 crore contract was not at risk from four weeks of delay; it was at risk from a second failed pilot. She switched models and kept the keyword path, and she made the evaluation set a standing asset — re-run on every change, owned by the product team rather than by engineering, because the question it answers is a product question. What to learn next follows directly: vector search and similarity, which covers how the index finds neighbours quickly among crores of vectors and what approximation costs you; and chunking and retrieval quality, which is where, on the evidence above, more of the improvement actually lives.

Two questions to sit with. First: if similarity is a verdict by a model rather than a property of your content, who in your organisation is accountable for that verdict — and would they recognise the description? Second: what would it cost you, in rupees and in days, to discover next quarter that you chose the wrong embedding model this quarter, and does anyone currently know that number?

Parakh Support Cloud: Which Model Decides What "Similar" Means?

Chennai, 22 September 2026. A support-automation company has twelve days to choose an embedding model before the festive quarter freezes its release calendar — and nobody in the room can say what the current one thinks a Hinglish complaint is about.

1. The decision

Kavya Srinivasan reached the Parakh Support Cloud office in Guindy at ten past eight on the morning of Monday, 22 September 2026, because the Toronto call had run past midnight and she had wanted the whiteboard to herself before anyone else arrived. On it she wrote three dates. 3 October: the last day on which a change to the search model could be re-indexed and tested before the engineering freeze. 11 October: Navratri, when the ticket volumes of Parakh's direct-to-consumer customers began their annual climb. 8 November: Diwali, when they peaked at roughly four times the ordinary day, and when nothing at all would be shipped.

Below the dates she wrote the number 31, and circled it. Thirty-one per cent was the share of Parakh's AI-suggested replies that support agents actually used. Fourteen months earlier, when the feature launched, the company's own business case had assumed 55 per cent. Kavya had to choose, by 3 October, between three ways of fixing it, and the three ways cost ₹31 lakh, ₹1.2 crore and almost nothing respectively.

2. The company

Parakh Support Cloud sells a customer-support helpdesk to Indian consumer brands. A shopper writes in about a delayed order or a faulty product; the ticket lands in Parakh; an agent replies. The company was started in 2019 by two former enterprise-software engineers who had watched Indian direct-to-consumer brands — the wave that followed the success of firms such as Nykaa, boAt and Lenskart — outgrow shared email inboxes without being able to afford the global helpdesk products priced in dollars. Parakh priced in rupees, supported eleven Indian languages, and integrated on day one with the tools those brands actually used: Shiprocket for logistics, Razorpay for payments, WhatsApp Business for the channel where most Indian consumers preferred to complain.

By September 2026 Parakh had 310 brand customers, annual recurring revenue of ₹41 crore, and 2.7 crore resolved tickets in storage. Its competition was partly domestic — the Indian SaaS incumbents that Freshworks and Zoho had made respectable — and partly the global suites. Its differentiation was language: a Parakh agent handling a queue for a Coimbatore textile brand saw tickets in English, in Tamil script, and above all in the transliterated Hinglish and Tanglish that Indian consumers write when they are annoyed. "Order kab tak aayega, 10 din ho gaye, please cancel karo" was a normal sentence.

The AI feature, launched in July 2025, was called Suggested Reply. When a new ticket arrived, Parakh converted the ticket text into an embedding — a fixed-length list of 768 numbers produced by a hosted model — and searched the brand's own archive of resolved tickets for the three whose embeddings sat closest to it. Those three, plus the replies that had resolved them, were passed to a language model that drafted an answer. The agent could accept, edit or ignore it.

3. What has happened

The overall acceptance rate of 31 per cent had been stable for four months, and Kavya had spent August discovering that the average concealed the story. Aravind Menon's team in Bengaluru broke the number down by the script and language of the incoming ticket, and the breakdown is Exhibit 1. Tickets written in ordinary English were accepted at 44 per cent — below target but respectable. Tickets in transliterated Hinglish were accepted at 19 per cent. Tickets in Tamil or Telugu script were accepted at 12 per cent.

Rhea Kapoor, Parakh's only data scientist, working from Toronto and therefore joining every Indian standup at eleven at night, had put the mechanism plainly on the previous week's call. The hosted embedding model Parakh used had been trained overwhelmingly on English web text, with some clean, formal Hindi in Devanagari script and very little of anything else. It had almost certainly never seen "kab tak aayega" written in Latin letters at scale. Its tokeniser broke such phrases into fragments it did not recognise, and the vector it produced was, in Rhea's words, "a shrug of the right length."

The consequence showed up in a small experiment she ran on 480 Hinglish tickets, summarised in Exhibit 3. For a query reading "order cancel karna hai, wrong size aaya", the current model's nearest stored ticket was an English ticket about order cancellation policy — reasonable — but its second and third neighbours were tickets about the word size in the sense of packaging dimensions, and the actual best answer, a resolved Hinglish ticket about a wrong-size exchange, ranked eleventh. A candidate multilingual model ranked that same ticket first.

Two other facts pressed on the decision. Wei-Ling Tan, the customer-success lead in Singapore, managed Parakh's largest single account: Miraaj Retail Group, a Dubai-based retail group running eleven brands across the Gulf, worth ₹4.6 crore a year and up for renewal on 30 November. Miraaj's queues were Arabic and English, and its acceptance rate was 16 per cent. And Doug Feinberg, who ran sales from New Jersey and sold Parakh to the Indian-diaspora-founded brands in North America, had already put "next-generation multilingual AI" on a January conference agenda.

4. The people

Aravind Menon, Engineering Manager, Bengaluru, wanted the vendor's newer multilingual embedding model. His argument was that it was a configuration change plus a re-index, that his team had shipped two such migrations before, and that the twelve days available were enough for exactly this and nothing more ambitious. What he did not emphasise was that his team's on-call rota during the festive quarter left no capacity for a rollback.

Rhea Kapoor, Data Scientist, Toronto, wanted a labelled evaluation set before any model was chosen. Her position was that Parakh had no way to tell whether a new model was better, only whether it was different, and that the 480-ticket experiment she had run was too small and had been labelled by her alone. She estimated three weeks and two annotators to build a set of 500 tickets across five languages, with the correct archive match marked by a person who had actually handled such queues.

Wei-Ling Tan, Customer Success Lead, Singapore, wanted anything demonstrable before 30 November. She had been in Dubai in August; Miraaj's head of customer operations had shown her a screen of Arabic tickets with suggestions in English, and had asked, politely, whether Parakh had tested the feature in Arabic at all. Wei-Ling had not been able to say yes.

Doug Feinberg, VP Sales, New Jersey, wanted the upgrade and wanted it named. His compensation was weighted to new logos in the January–March quarter and he had a slide that said "multilingual by design." He was not opposed to Rhea's evaluation set; he simply did not see why it could not happen after the upgrade.

Exhibit 2 makes the trade visible. Option A is the only one that changes the model before the freeze, and it commits ₹96 lakh a year and nine days of re-indexing to a model that has never been measured on Parakh's own tickets. Option B is the only one that teaches a model what Parakh's queues actually look like, and it arrives after the quarter that matters.
