Exhibit 3 shows what "similar" means to each model, and it is the exhibit Kavya kept returning to. The current model is not malfunctioning: it is ranking by the English words it recognises — cancel, size, order — and treating the Hindi verbs as noise. That is a faithful expression of what it was trained on. The multilingual model puts the right ticket first. But the exhibit rests on 480 tickets from three apparel brands, labelled by one person, and says nothing about whether English acceptance would fall.

6. The options

Option A: switch models now. Re-embed all 2.7 crore tickets against the vendor's multilingual model, ship before the freeze, and let the festive quarter be the test. Upside: the segments that are failing are the ones the new model is built for, and Doug gets his announcement. Cost: ₹31 lakh now and ₹96 lakh a year, an unmeasured bet, and no capacity to roll back if English acceptance drops during the highest-volume weeks of the year.

Option B: fine-tune on Parakh's own data. Take an open multilingual model and train it on pairs of Parakh tickets that agents historically resolved with the same answer, which is a supply of labelled data no vendor has. Upside: the resulting model would understand Hinglish as Parakh's customers actually write it, and the annual run cost would fall to ₹38 lakh because the model would be self-hosted. Cost: ₹1.2 crore, fourteen weeks, a model Parakh must then operate, and delivery after Miraaj's renewal date.

Option C: measure first, and fix what is cheap. Spend three weeks building a 500-ticket labelled evaluation set across five languages with two annotators drawn from the customer-success team; in parallel, add a keyword path so that order numbers and tracking IDs are matched exactly, and let each brand upload a glossary of its own product names. Then choose between A and B in late October with evidence, and ship in December. Upside: ₹9 lakh, every later decision becomes cheap and defensible, and the keyword path is a known win. Cost: nothing visible improves before Diwali, and Wei-Ling walks into the Miraaj renewal with a plan rather than a product.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. In your own words, what is the current embedding model doing when it ranks "Package size is too big for my letterbox" second for a Hinglish cancellation request? Is this a bug?
  2. Exhibit 1 reports a blended acceptance rate of 31 per cent. What decisions would a manager make wrongly if they saw only that number, and what is the smallest change to the reporting that would prevent it?
  3. Exhibit 3 favours the multilingual model decisively. List three specific reasons why it is not sufficient evidence for a ₹96 lakh annual commitment, and say what evidence would be sufficient.
  4. Which option should Kavya choose by 3 October, and what exactly should Wei-Ling tell Miraaj Retail Group before 30 November?

8. A note for the learner

The lens this case is built around is the definition of an embedding: a fixed-length list of numbers representing a piece of content, positioned so that things the model treats as similar sit close together. The italicised words carry the case. There is no model-independent fact about whether "order cancel karna hai" is similar to "wrong size deliver hua hai". There is only a verdict, issued by a particular model that learned its notions of similarity from a particular pile of text. Parakh's model learned from English web pages. It is behaving correctly and serving the wrong customers.

Recognising this reframes the decision. It is not "our AI is underperforming, buy better AI." It is "we have delegated a judgement about our customers' language to a supplier who has never seen it, and we have no instrument that measures the judgement." A learner who reaches that framing will notice three consequences that the case supplies but does not spell out. First, the choice of model is a product decision about which customers get good service, not a technical preference. Second, Parakh cannot currently tell a better model from a different one, because it has no labelled set — which means Option A is not a fix but a swap of one unmeasured model for another. Third, the ₹31 lakh re-indexing line in Exhibit 2 is the price of every future change too, so each model choice silently sets the cost of the next one.

One defensible path runs as follows. Kavya takes Option C, with two amendments that answer the objections to it. She builds the evaluation set — three weeks, ₹9 lakh, annotators from customer success who have actually worked Hinglish queues — and ships the keyword path and per-brand glossaries before the freeze, because those are cheap, low-risk and disproportionately helpful for the order-number and product-name queries that make up a large share of festive volume. She then runs both candidate models against the evaluation set in late October while the freeze holds, so that the decision on 1 December is made with numbers rather than with Exhibit 3.

For Miraaj, she does not promise a model. She commits to a specific, dated measurement: Parakh will report Arabic-language retrieval accuracy against a labelled set of Miraaj's own tickets by 15 November, with the remediation plan attached. That is a stronger renewal argument than an untested upgrade, because it answers the question Miraaj actually asked — have you tested this in Arabic? — with a yes and a date, rather than with a new model that has also not been tested in Arabic.

The reasoning behind the path is that Parakh's binding constraint is not model quality but the absence of measurement, and that spending ₹96 lakh a year to resolve an argument that ₹9 lakh of labelling would settle is the more expensive kind of speed. The path has a real cost, and a learner should say so plainly: nothing user-visible improves during the festive quarter, Doug's January slide loses its headline, and if the multilingual model would in fact have worked, Parakh has left three months of better service on the table. That is the trade. What makes the path defensible is not that it is safe but that, at the end of it, Parakh knows something it does not know today.
